title: Terms should be defined once at a location covering all their uses, not repeated per document
content:
A.1.2.2.2.22 states the placement rule for Definition Documents: "To the extent possible it should be avoided to have the same term defined multiple times in the Atlas, and instead always put a single definition at a location in the Atlas that covers all of its use. The main exception to this principle should be when relatively niche terms are present in two different Scopes."

This is a normalization rule with a governance rationale rather than a tidiness rationale. Duplicate definitions in a tree where higher documents govern the interpretation of lower ones create a live hazard: two copies drift apart, and then which copy applies becomes an argument about tree position rather than about meaning. Because contradictions between Atlas Documents are a defect the Core Facilitator must expend interpretation authority to repair (A.1.1.2.1), every duplicated definition is a pre-loaded contradiction.

"A location that covers all of its use" is the operative instruction and it is a real constraint: it forces a definition **upward** to the common ancestor of every document that uses the term. Defining a widely-used term locally is a placement error even if the text is correct.

The Scope-crossing exception is the pragmatic limit. The common ancestor of two Scopes is the Atlas root, and hoisting a niche term into the Immutable layers to avoid duplication would be far worse than two copies — it would make a minor term permanent. So the rule yields where normalization would collide with the mutability hierarchy.
description: A.1.2.2.2.22 makes single-definition placement the rule, with the sole sanctioned exception being niche terms appearing in two different Scopes.
